hints: Compare the sizes of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ down Group 2 and think what this means for charge density.
Think how strongly each cation can distort the electron cloud of the large $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion and weaken a C-O bond.
walkthrough:
Picture what thermal decomposition does**
Think of $\text{MCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$. You are not just heating a solid, you are breaking the carbonate ion apart to release $\text{CO}_2$. Anything that already weakens the carbonate makes this easier, so it decomposes at a lower temperature.

Compare the two cations**
Both ions are $2+$, but $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is small while $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much larger because barium is further down Group 2 with an extra electron shell. Same charge spread over a larger volume means $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ has a much lower charge density and lower polarising power.

Link polarising power to stability**
A small highly polarising $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ pulls strongly on the electron cloud of $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, distorting it and weakening one of the C-O bonds. This helps the carbonate break up. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ distorts $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ much less, so $\text{BaCO}_3$ is more thermally stable and needs stronger heating before it begins to decompose.

Final answer: $\text{BaCO}_3$ / barium carbonate requires the higher temperature.
$\text{Ba}^{2+}$ has a larger ionic radius and smaller charge density than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, so it polarises / distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion less and the C-O bond is weakened less.

hints: Write what forms when the oxide dissolves and then $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is added, and identify the two possible sulfate precipitates $\text{CaSO}_4$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$.
Recall how solubility of Group 2 sulfates changes down the group and which sulfate will stay in solution longer.
Think of dissolving as $\Delta H_{sol} \approx -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$, and consider which term falls more rapidly with larger cations.
walkthrough:
Work out what is in the beaker**
$\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and similarly $\text{BaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2$. Both dissolve with no solid present. Adding $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ supplies $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, so the possible precipitates are $\text{CaSO}_4$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$: $$\text{M}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{MSO}_4(\text{s})$$

Use the sulfate solubility trend**
Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases sharply down the group. $\text{CaSO}_4$ is sparingly soluble but $\text{BaSO}_4$ is essentially insoluble. That means a barium solution precipitates almost immediately with a drop of acid, while a calcium solution can hold much more $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ before $\text{CaSO}_4$ appears, so the calcium sample needs most acid.

Explain with energetics**
Whether $\text{MSO}_4$ dissolves depends on breaking the lattice ($\Delta H_{latt}$) and hydrating the gaseous ions ($\Delta H_{hyd}$). For the large $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ion, $\Delta H_{latt}$ changes relatively little from $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. In contrast $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of $\text{M}^{2+}$ becomes much less exothermic because $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is larger and less strongly attracted to water. The hydration term dominates, so solution of $\text{BaSO}_4$ is less favourable and it is less soluble.

Final answer: The calcium oxide / calcium hydroxide sample requires most sulfuric acid.
$\text{CaSO}_4$ is more soluble than $\text{BaSO}_4$.
Both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of the sulfate become less exothermic down the group, but the change in $\Delta H_{hyd}$ is dominant / greater, so dissolving becomes less favourable for $\text{BaSO}_4$.

hints: Use the 1:1 mole ratio $\text{CaCO}_3 : \text{CO}_2$ and the relation mass = moles $\times$ $M_r$ with $M_r$ of $\text{CO}_2$ = 44.
walkthrough:
Convert moles of gas to mass**
The decomposition is $$\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$$ so 0.02 mol carbonate gives 0.02 mol $\text{CO}_2$. Mass follows $m = n \times M_r$: $$m = 0.02 \times 44 = 0.88 \text{ g}$$

hints: Write the balanced complete combustion equation for propane, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and note how many moles of $\text{CO}_2$ come from one mole of propane.
Divide the moles of $\text{CO}_2$ from (c)(i) by 3 to get moles of propane, then multiply by $M_r$ of propane, 44.
walkthrough:
Find moles of propane needed**
Complete combustion is $$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ One mole of propane makes three moles of $\text{CO}_2$. You need 0.02 mol $\text{CO}_2$, so: $$n(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8) = \frac{0.02}{3} = 0.006666... \text{ mol}$$

Convert to mass to 3 significant figures**
$M_r$ of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 = (3 \times 12.0) + (8 \times 1.0) = 44.0$. Then: $$m = n \times M_r = \frac{0.02}{3} \times 44.0 = 0.293 \text{ g}$$ Keep three significant figures as requested.

Final answer: moles of propane = $0.02 / 3$ = 0.00667 mol
mass of propane = $0.02 / 3 \times 44$ = 0.293 g (3 s.f.)
